news.abstract: How do you mark the passage of 1,000 years of human history? Simple in Hong Kong, a city of chronic gamblers and cold-eyed oddsmakers: you head for the track.    At 12:45 a.m., as the last wisps of smoke from New Year's Eve fireworks drifted away from the Happy Valley Racecourse, the crack of a starter's gun set off the Millennium Cup.
news.title: A Day at the Races, A Night of Big Parties

news.abstract: Pakistan's government welcomes freeing of passengers held hostage aboard hijacked Indian Airlines plane in Afghanistan and praises that country's Taliban leaders for the way they managed the crisis (M)
news.title: Pakistan Welcomes Hijacking's End and Praises the Taliban

news.abstract: At the last minute, Hungary's millennium planners turned into the Not-Ready-for-Prime-Time Players.    Two unusual events had been set for midnight: the first spin of a giant Wheel of Time holding an hourglass containing seven tons of customized sand, and a special session of Parliament to celebrate 1,000 years of Hungarian statehood.
news.title: Well, Let's Try Again, Maybe Dec. 31, 2000

news.abstract: More and 150 people held hostage on a hijacked Indian Airlines plane for eight days arrive safely in New Delhi from Afghanistan after India secures their freedom by agreeing to release three jailed militants; five hijackers leave plan in Kandahar, Afghanistan, where they are joined by the released militants, who include a Muslim cleric named Maulana Masood Azhar; analysts say hijacking may have long-term political consequences in region, helping to legitimize Taliban, Afghan group that helped to end crisis, and further souring relations between India and Pakistan, which Indian officials and press have portrayed as hidden hand behind the hijacking; criticism in India over government's handling of hijacking intensifies in hours after hostages' release militants; photos (M)
news.title: Hostages Land in India After Deal Is Made With Hijackers

news.abstract: EUROPE    FRANCE: MORE EXPLOSIVES LINKED TO BASQUES  The French police have seized a ton of explosives they said belonged to the Spanish Basque separatist guerrilla group E.T.A., a week after two powerful van bombs were found and defused in Spain. The explosives were found in an unused garage outside the city of Pau near the Spanish border.    Suzanne Daley (NYT)    BRITAIN: HONORS FOR ACTORS  Elizabeth Taylor, Julie Andrews and Sean Connery have new titles: Dame Elizabeth, Dame Julie and Sir Sean. The three actors were among 2,000 people honored in the annual New Year's list drawn up by the government and bestowed by the queen. Also honored were sports heroes, milkmen, crossing guards and the multimillionaire head of the Virgin Group, now Sir Richard Branson.   (AP)    AFRICA    SUDAN: CABINET QUITS  Three weeks after declaring a state of emergency, President Omar el-Bashir said he had accepted his cabinet's resignation, paving the way for him to consolidate his power. In a speech marking Sudan's 44th anniversary of independence, Mr. Bashir said ministers and state governors had expressed their desire to resign and he had accepted their resignations. However, he asked them to stay on as caretakers until he could reform the cabinet.   (AP)    NIGER: PREMIER AGAIN  A former prime minister, Hama Amadou, 49, was reappointed to the position by President Mamadou Tandja, who was sworn in on Dec. 22. Mr. Amadou also held the title in 1995, under President Mahamane Ousmane, who is now parliamentary speaker.    (Agence France-Presse)    CONGO: REBELS TELL OF AMBUSH  Rebels killed about 80 government soldiers in an ambush, a rebel leader said, a day after Congolese representatives held an unsuccessful meeting with a rebel envoy. Jean-Pierre Bemba, whose Congolese Liberation Movement is fighting to topple President Laurent Kabila with Ugandan backing, said government troops had been ambushed along the Congo River.    (AP)    ASIA    SRI LANKA: REBELS REPULSED  Troops repulsed Tamil Tiger rebels trying to overrun defenses at a key northern military base, the defense ministry said. The ministry said 9 soldiers and 9 rebels had been killed and 41 soldiers hurt, although independent confirmation of the figures was not possible.    (Reuters)    EAST TIMOR: U.N. AIDE APOLOGIZES  The United Nations administrator in East Timor apologized for its failure to predict and prevent a wave of violence after the territory's overwhelming vote for independence from Indonesia. Sergio Vieira de Mello, who is overseeing East Timor's transition to independence, made the apology during a visit to the coffee-growing area of Ermera, said the United Nations spokesman Fred Eckhard.   (AP)    EAST TIMOR: GUSMAO RULES HIMSELF OUT  Jose Alexandre Gusmao said he foresaw full independence for East Timor in at most two years but that he did not plan to become its first president. Mr. Gusmao had been widely expected to become an independent East Timor's first leader, but said he intended to signal that leaders of the independence struggle did not have an automatic right to power.    (Agence France-Presse)    THE AMERICAS    HONDURAS, NICARAGUA: MILITARY PACT  Honduras and Nicaragua have agreed to freeze ground troop deployments and withdraw naval forces from the Caribbean Sea to avert military conflict pending resolution of a border dispute, an official with the Organization of American States said. Relations soured in November when the Honduran Congress ratified an accord that claimed for Honduras and Colombia 52,000 square miles of Caribbean coastal waters, parts of which are also claimed by Nicaragua.    (Reuters)    PARAGUAY: CABINET MINISTER QUITS  Agriculture Minister Oscar Denis quit after his Liberal Party voted to abandon the coalition government of President Luis Gonzalez Macchi. The party's leadership voted to pull out after talks to obtain more government posts failed. The decision faces ratification by party members at a convention in February.    (Reuters)    COLOMBIA: LEADER VETOES GENOCIDE BILL  In an unex-pected reversal, President Andres Pastrana vetoed a bill that would have made genocide and forced disappearance criminal acts. His administration shifted course after the armed forces complained that such a law would leave soldiers open to prosecution, in civilian rather than military courts, for deaths inflicted in combat with leftist guerrillas.    Larry Rohter (NYT)    MIDDLE EAST    IRAN: CALL TO DESTROY ISRAEL  Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader, called for the destruction of Israel, saying it was the only way to solve the Middle East's problems. His remarks came as millions of people rallied across Iran to protest Israel's control of Jerusalem, where Muslims believe Muhammad began his journey to heaven.    (AP)    LEBANON: HEZBOLLAH'S VOW  The Hezbollah movement said it intended to keep up its attacks on Israeli troops in south Lebanon, a day after a suicide bombing narrowly missed an Israeli patrol near the village of Qlaia, wounding 12 Lebanese civilians and an Israeli soldier. ''Hezbollah operations will not stop before or after the negotiations'' between Israel and Syria, a Hezbollah press official said.    (Agence France-Presse)
news.title: World Briefing

news.abstract: Family cats are being stolen in Beijing to meet the demand for cat meat in Cantonese-style restaurants, which have been opening up across the city (M)
news.title: Diners's Taste Leads to Cat-Nabbing in Beijing

news.abstract: Passengers and crew kept hostage for eight days aboard a hijacked Indian Airlines jetliner describe days of tedium and moments of terror; talk of living with stench of overflowing toilets and of deciding to stop eating solid foods in an effort to avoid the dreaded bathrooms; some admit to strange bond they formed with one hijacker, who was the most sympathetic and solicitous until the day he told them that they would all be killed; photos (M)
news.title: Hostages Recall Times of Terror Amid Boredom

news.abstract: Law enforcement and intelligence officials in US and around the world remain on high state of alert because of possibility of terrorism, even as they express relief that year 2000 began without any sign of significant disruption caused by criminal or extremist groups (M)
news.title: With Fears Of Terrorism, Precautions Will Continue

news.abstract: Acting Pres Vladimir V Putin celebrates New Year with Russian troops fighting in Chechnya; visit offers nation used to Boris N Yeltsin a new image of an active, concerned leader and reflects Putin's close association with Chechnya battle; his success in presidential elections now scheduled for March 26 could well hinge on success of campaign; photo (M)
news.title: IN A BUSY START, NEW RUSSIA LEADER GOES TO CHECHNYA

news.abstract: Grozny, capital of Chechnya, becomes a deadly killing zone as Russian troops run into fierce resistance from heavily armed, experienced and motivated rebels; make inroads, but still do not control city center; official casuality figures understate Russian losses, which are estimated at 10 soldiers a day; popularity of Vladimir V Putin, acting president, is based in large part reports of low casualties; photos; map (M)
news.title: Chechnya's Capital Becomes A Deadly Zone for Russians

news.abstract: It was only when Mario Fernandez saw the headline, ''Pinochet Under Arrest,'' that the dam broke and he finally found it possible to talk about the beatings, the electric shocks, the cigarette burns, the terrible sense of humiliation and alienation.    ''My body froze; I had an intense allergic reaction, and I didn't know whether to laugh or cry,'' said Mr. Fernandez, trembling at the memory. He ran to his wife and wept on her shoulder, and, at long last, took her advice to seek therapy.
news.title: SHADOWS OF TORMENT/A special report.; Pinochet Case Reviving Voices of the Tortured

news.abstract: For much of his presidency, Bill Clinton's own aides have frequently complained that his attention to foreign policy was sporadic. The trait got him in trouble in Bosnia, and often resulted in some nasty surprises -- from the defeat of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty last fall to a tear-gas-filled week in Seattle that badly damaged his global economic agenda.    But some of his biggest victories in 1999 were also scored abroad, from the air campaign over Serbia that largely halted ethnic bloodshed to the Northern Ireland accord that offers the first prospect of peace there.
news.title: Clinton's Final Chapter: Single-Minded, Full-Steam Run at a Global Agenda

news.abstract: Eighteen months ago the Pentagon strongly opposed a plan to create a permanent international criminal tribunal, fearing that a strong and independent court would expose American troops sent overseas to prosecution outside the American judicial system.    Now, as a result of NATO's air war against the Serbs last spring, members of the American military have already undergone the scrutiny of just such a court: the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. Experts on international law say that may create political and legal precedents for requiring Americans to submit to international judicial review.
news.title: Kosovo Inquiry Confirms U.S. Fears of War Crimes Court

news.abstract: As president, Carlos Saul Menem dominated Argentine news coverage for more than a decade by selling off much of the government and pegging the peso to the dollar -- not to mention racing sports cars, throwing his wife out of the presidential palace and dating women half his age.     Now out of power for barely three weeks, Mr. Menem has managed to remain at the center of attention. He has sometimes even managed to overshadow the always demure President Fernando de la Rua, who campaigned promising a new style of government.
news.title: Argentina's Former President Still at Center Stage

news.abstract: Having done little more than break the ice in their first encounter last month, Israeli and Syrian leaders enter knottier terrain on Monday as they resume American-brokered negotiations ambitiously aimed at reaching a peace accord by the summer.    The mere fact of their meeting was achievement enough when the Israelis and the Syrians revived their peace effort in December after a four-year stalemate. This time the two sides will be forced to tackle directly the tangle of issues that have bedeviled their previous efforts at peacemaking: borders, security and the opening of normal relations.
news.title: ISRAEL AND SYRIA MEET TODAY IN U.S. ON TANGLED ISSUES

news.abstract: Acting President Vladimir V. Putin began to put his own imprint on the Kremlin administration today, showing the door to Tatyana Dyachenko, who wielded considerable influence in the administration of her father, Boris N. Yeltsin.    Mr. Putin also moved aside several other staff members who had been loyal to Mr. Yeltsin. But as one television commentator said tonight, the changes amount to a ''freshening up'' of the administration rather than a revolution inside the Kremlin.
news.title: Putin Takes Charge, Firing Yeltsin's Daughter and Others

news.abstract: Looking Ahead to Century 21
news.title: Growing Market Offers Huge Potential — but Also Peril : Globalization's Double Edge

news.abstract: EUROPE    BRITAIN: NAZI SUSPECT DEPORTED -- Britain ordered the deportation to Australia of Konrad Kalejs, 86, suspected of being a Nazi death squad officer responsible for the murder of up to 30,000 Jews, Communists and Gypsies in Latvia in World War II. Mr. Kalejs, an Australian citizen of Latvian descent, was found living in a retirement home in England. The police said they had no grounds for arresting Mr. Kalejs and Australia said it had already decided not to prosecute him.   Sarah Lyall (NYT)    FRANCE: OUSTED PRESIDENT ARRIVES -- The former President of the Ivory Coast, Henri Konan Bedie, who was ousted in a military coup on Dec. 24, arrived in Paris. He had been staying in Togo since the coup and flew into Orly airport aboard the Togolese presidential jet. Togolese officials said Mr. Bedie, who has an apartment in Paris, is expected to take up residence there.   Suzanne Daley (NYT)
news.title: WORLD BRIEFING

news.abstract: Alan Jolis, 46, the author most recently of "Love and Terror," a historical novel set during the French Revolution, died Thursday at his home in Sweden after a long struggle with brain cancer.
news.title: OBITUARY : Alan Jolis, 46, Author

news.abstract: Slumped in the shadow of a mud wall, any desire he might have had to stand up drained by the midday sun and the Ramadan fast, Mamadou Tombo explained the simple truth about his village of rice farmers.    ''When there was good flood and rain,'' said Mr. Tombo, the mayor, ''there was no exodus.''
news.title: Gomitogo Journal; Undependable Rains Bring Seasonal Exodus

news.abstract: Israel will transfer another chunk of the West Bank to the Palestinians by Thursday after negotiators resolved a lingering dispute over the land today, ending a stalemate that had dispirited both sides.    After the maps were signed tonight, Israel was expected to turn over 5 percent of the West Bank to the Palestinian Authority within 48 hours. Most of the land is an unpopulated swath of the Judean Desert.
news.title: Israel to Give Palestinians Another Piece Of West Bank

news.abstract: The nagging question today, as Russian officials began laboriously assembling the machinery for Russia's second post-Soviet presidential election, was not how or when the vote would be held. It was why.    With less than 12 weeks remaining until the likeliest election date in late March, not a single serious politician has firmly committed to running against acting President Vladimir V. Putin. Commentators are rating the prospects of anyone who does as close to zero.
news.title: Russia's Presidential Race Lacks Runners

news.abstract: President Clinton made a second trip here today, breaking an impasse between Syria and Israel over the agenda for their peace talks and convening the first face-to-face talks between Prime Minister Ehud Barak of Israel and Foreign Minister Farouk al-Shara of Syria.     Mr. Clinton's reappearance in this small West Virginia town came after Israeli and Syrian negotiators bogged down in a dispute over whether the first topic of discussion would be Syria's demand for the return of the Golan Heights, which Israel has controlled since the 1967 Middle East war, or Israel's search for security guarantees.
news.title: Clinton Breaks an Impasse At the Israel-Syria Talks

news.abstract: Croatia's center-left opposition won a sweeping victory in parliamentary elections on Monday, official results indicated today. The elections delivered a rebuke to the governing party and opens up the prospect of much warmer ties with the West.    The opposition victory dethroned the Croatian Democratic Union, the umbrella nationalist party founded by Franjo Tudjman, the president who died last month. The party has ruled Croatia since Mr. Tudjman took the country to independence in 1991 out of the wreckage of Tito's Yugoslavia.
news.title: Pro-Western Opposition Defeats Croatia's Ruling Nationalists

news.abstract: The two old men live in a small research center in this stunning mountain town, translating religious scriptures of their minority culture from a pictographic script that almost nobody else can fully decipher anymore.    These men are the last of the dongba -- priests of the Naxi people who have lived in Lijiang and the surrounding mountains of southwestern China with their own animist religion and writing system for more than 1,000 years. Now they are helping to compile an accessible record of their sacred knowledge before it dies out altogether.
news.title: Lijiang Journal; A Dying Culture, as Seen Through Aging Eyes

news.abstract: In some of the sharpest market movements since the Asian financial crisis ended last year, stock prices across Asia and Europe plunged Wednesday in response to major falls in U.S. markets Tuesday.
news.title: Dow Rebounds as World Watches : Asian Markets Join European Sell-Off

news.abstract: In the midst of the euphoria and high expectations following their convincing victory in parliamentary elections on Monday, leaders of Croatia's democratic opposition are growing concerned about when they will be able to take power and what they will find when they do so.     Ivica Racan, the moderate former Communist who will become the country's new prime minister, said in an interview today that it could be a month or more before Croatia's cumbersome constitutional process  allows him to form a government.
news.title: Croatian Victors Fret About What Awaits Them

news.abstract: On the third day of talks, Israeli and Syrian officials today slowly began tackling specific questions of how they might normalize relations.    They also took up security arrangements, with an eye to persuading Israeli voters to approve a return of the Golan Heights.
news.title: In No Hurry, Israel-Syria Talks Edge Toward Specifics

news.abstract: Encircled by Russian forces and subjected to constant bombardment, Chechen rebels in Grozny have begun to lash back, forcing furious firefights on the outskirts of the city.    Rebel officials asserted today that they had left their hiding places in Grozny and seized the village of Alkhan-Kala, on the southwestern outskirts of the Chechen capital, according to independent media outlets in Russia.
news.title: Chechen Rebels Fiercely Attack Russian Forces

news.abstract: Angered by several bombings in Cape Town and frustrated by the difficulties in solving such cases, South Africa is considering constitutional changes that would curb the rights of suspected terrorists.    The country's safety and security minister, Steve Tshwete, wants the police to have the power to hold such suspects without charges for more than the 48 hours now allowed and wants to curtail their access to lawyers, law enforcement officials say.
news.title: Crime Kindles Rights Debate In South Africa

news.abstract: On his knees, the herald bent toward the acting chief, fingering his gift of a whale's tooth as he murmured the standard apologies of greeting.    He had come, he said, to introduce a foreigner who asked leave to wander around the village, and begged forgiveness in advance for any breaches of protocol.
news.title: Somosomo Journal; Island of the Endless Smile, but With Sharks, Too

news.abstract: India today intensified its efforts to blame Pakistan for the Indian Airlines hijacking, announcing that four accomplices had been seized in Bombay and that they had identified the five hijackers as Pakistanis and acknowledged official Pakistani sponsorship of the hijacking.    The home minister, Lal Krishna Advani, said at a news conference here that the statements of the four reported accomplices -- an Indian, two Pakistanis and a Nepali -- and other ''telltale pointers'' conclusively established Pakistan's role in the seizure of the Airbus. The plane was hijacked as it flew from Katmandu, Nepal, to New Delhi on Dec. 24 with 178 passengers and 11 crew members on board.
news.title: INDIA  INTENSIFIES HIJACKING DISPUTE

news.abstract: PARIS—  For a good part of the last two decades, France has lived with a nasty, neo-fascist pustule in a highly visible place: R1 Rouge, a section of grandstand virtually turned into an enclave for young, right-wing extremists at Parc des Princes, the soccer stadium of Paris St. Germain.
news.title: Paris Soccer Team Struggles to De-Nazify a Cheering Section

news.abstract: Boris N. Yeltsin's first pilgrimage to the Holy Land offered up a series of curious juxtapositions today: the man who entered politics as a Communist received a high honor from a senior Orthodox cleric; Russia's first president pronounced his historically anti-Semitic land free of anti-Jewish sentiment; the convert to democracy who has just quit politics sat at lunch opposite Natan Sharansky, a major political force in Israel, who spent nine years in Soviet jails defending freedoms that Mr. Yeltsin only later brought to his country.    Everywhere he went, Mr. Yeltsin was treated like the head of state he so recently was, before his stunning resignation on New Year's Eve. And everywhere, church and political leaders eagerly sought his embrace.
news.title: Yeltsin's Visit To Holy Land Is a Portrait Of Paradox

news.abstract: In a move that the Vatican says will damage efforts to mend its relations with Beijing, China's state-sanctioned Catholic Church consecrated five new bishops here today, just hours before Pope John Paul II consecrated 12 bishops at St. Peter's Basilica.    The two-hour ceremony, on a wintry morning in the unheated Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception here, adhered closely to the rites of a traditional Catholic consecration. But the bishops, who range in age from 35 to 73, were appointed not by the Vatican, but by the Patriotic Catholic Association -- a sort of parallel church that answers to the Chinese government.
news.title: Beijing-Backed Church, Defying Vatican, Installs 5 New Bishops

news.abstract: After years of rapid growth, U.S. waste-recycling efforts are leveling off. The percentage of municipal solid waste diverted to recycling rose from 10 percent in 1980 to 28.8 percent in 1998 before flattening out, The Washington Post reports.
news.title: Short Takes

news.abstract: Pres Clinton intervenes in Israeli-Syrian peace talks, offering seven-page 'working paper' defining differences over deal that would return Golan Heights to Syria; acts after American officials find that Israeli Prime Min Ehud Barak and Syrian Min Farouk al-Shara have sufficiently shown to domestic constituencies that they are holding out on key issues; photo (M)
news.title: Clinton Offers Israel and Syria 7-Page 'Working Paper' to Study Golan Heights Control

news.abstract: SINGAPORE—  Tens of thousands of Indonesian Muslims demonstrated in Jakarta on Friday for the third day in a row to press the government to end sectarian violence in the Moluccan Islands.
news.title: Thousands Protesting In Indonesia Threaten An Islamic Holy War : Muslims Call On Jakarta To Intervene In Moluccas

news.abstract: Prince Yevgeny A Meshchersky and family have been squatting for three years in ruined gatehouse, Alabino, Russia, in bid to reclaim ancestral 64-acre estate; authorities have done nothing to evict him or to give him property he claims; he comments, interview; map; photo (M)
news.title: In Ancestral Russia Ruins, Family Asserts Its Rights

news.abstract: Clinton administration officials and scientists who have toured Vector, Siberian lab formerly used by Soviet Union to develop viral weapons, say quiet United States aid to convert lab to peaceful research seems to be paying off; some American intelligence analysts and Congressional staff members remain wary; photo (M)
news.title: U.S. Helps Russia Turn Germ Center to Peace Uses

news.abstract: Joaquin Lavin, first conservative candidate with chance to win Chile's presidency since Gen Augusto Pinochet left power in 1990, has softened image of country's right wing, which still carries baggage of human rights abuses of Pinochet dictatorship; Lavin, mayor of Las Condes, is part of new wave of younger politicians who appear committed to overturning traditionally highly centralized power structures of Latin y America, parlaying local government success into capturing national attention, and even high office; photo (M)
news.title: Chilean's Homespun Record Could Make Him President

news.abstract: Recent study commissioned by Czech daily indicates that almost half of working women in Czech Republic have been subjected to sexual harassment in workplace; reports from other post-Communist countries indicate that sexual harassment, though seldom identified as such, is widespread; in Czech Republic, 45 percent of women say they were sexually harassed, many of them repeatedly; women's rights advocates say real figures are probably higher; note that term often used by Czechs for sexual harassment, translated, means 'sexual buzz,' with tacit understanding that whoever complains about harassment is making unnecessary fuss (M)
news.title: Czech Poll: Harassment Of Women Is Common

news.abstract: Pres Fernando Henrique Cardoso summons lawmakers back to Brasilia for special session to consider his 2000 budget; congressional leaders, mindful of local elections, have dismissed his austerity package and countered with proposals of their own that would limit presidential powers and dip further into federal purse; just one year ago, currency crisis in Brazil sparked fears that country's economy was headed toward meltdown; growth has resumed, and it is once again business as usual in Congress (M)
news.title: After Crisis, Reform Bills Languish In Brazil

news.abstract: Acting Pres Vladimir V Putin says decision to suspend Russia's bombardment of Grozny was taken to spare civilians and to honor Orthodox and Muslim holidays; Putin's reasons for halting bombardment are different from military's, suggesting that announcement is at least partly matter of packaging and public relations; suspension appears to be prelude to even more furious assault on Chechen capital; photo (M)
news.title: As Russian Army Rests, New Spins Offered for Lull in Grozny

news.abstract: State Under Seige, special report on how illicit drug trade now defines lives of residents of Baja California; for many years Mexicans believed that drugs like cocaine merely passed through their country en route to United States; now street crime, fed by explosion of drug abuse, has risen exponentially in Tijuana and elsewhere; police are overwhelmed by drug-related killings and courts awash in traffickers' bribes; crimes like kidnappings, bank robberies and drive-by shootings are commonplace; public safety is biggest concern of citizens; they thought that 10 years ago, when they voted out corrupt political machine, there would be new era; but waves of drug-related crime that coincided with more democratic politics is eroding their faith that any government can improve their lives; major presidential candidates cite collapsing justice system as crucial issue, but they say little to sustain faith in power of free political choice; photos; map (L)
news.title: STATE UNDER SIEGE: A special report.; Mexican Tale of Absolute Drug Corruption

news.abstract: Hans Schwerte, an authority on literary history who admitted in 1995 that under another name he had been an SS officer, died on Dec. 18 in a retirement home in Marquartstein, Germany. He was 90. His death was announced by the Aachen Technical University.     By the time that he acknowledged his SS role under his original name, Hans-Ernst Schneider, Dr. Schwerte had retired as a professor at the university, where he was rector from 1970 to 1973, and had received a high German decoration for his postwar contributions to German scholarship.
news.title: Hans Schwerte, 90, Ex-SS Man Who Hid Identity

news.abstract: A spate of reports in the German press suggested this weekend that President Vladimir V. Putin was decorated for his work as a K.G.B. agent in East Germany during the 1980's, and was even expelled from West Germany at one point after being identified as a Soviet spy.     But beyond vague statements from German intelligence spokesmen, there was little to confirm the accounts. American intelligence officials, speaking privately, have said that to their knowledge, Mr. Putin's 15-year career as a K.G.B. agent was not exceptional.
news.title: Putin Was Once Decorated as a Spy; Few Agree on His Deeds

news.abstract: On what appeared to be the last full day of an initial round of peace talks between Israel and Syria, Prime Minister Ehud Barak of Israel on Sunday took a lengthy tour of the site of one of the deadliest  single confrontations in American history, the battle of Antietam, and spent the evening at a final dinner with President Clinton and Syria's foreign minister hashing out a path to an elusive peace deal.     Mr. Clinton's dinner and then separate meetings with the leaders lasted until 12:30 a.m. today, and as the president returned to the White House the State Department spokesman, James P. Rubin, said, ''All the issues came up at dinner.''
news.title: An 1862 Battle Offers Impetus for 'Tough' Mideast Talks

news.abstract: ''Artillery ready?'' Lt. Col. Yuri Budanov shouted.    ''On the planned targets!'' came the reply.
news.title: Russian Troops in Chechnya Find Little Quiet on the Southern Front

news.abstract: Leon Radzinowicz, a scholar of criminology who played a major role in the development of the field, died on Dec. 29 at his home in Haverford, Pa. He was 93.    For most of his career, Mr. Radzinowicz, who was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 1970, taught law at Cambridge University, where he also founded the Institute of Criminology in 1959; he retired in 1973 after serving as its first director.
news.title: Leon Radzinowicz, 93, Leader in Criminology

news.abstract: Analysts clash over images of North Korea's Rodong missile site taken by private spy satellite and quietly released last week by Space Imaging Inc; some dismiss site as surprisingly primitive, while others express concern that so little infrastructure is needed to launch deadly missiles; company president Jeffrey K Harris says first detailed public images of site contribute to informed debate; photos; map (M)
news.title: Spy Photos of Korea Missile Site Bring Dispute

news.abstract: Russian forces battle to restore control behind their front lines after surprise rebel attacks that apparently throw Russian forces off balance and raise questions about Russian strategy in Chechnya; Defense Min Igor Sergeyev ends suspension of air and artillery attacks on Grozny and resumes full-scale offensive; imposes evening curfew on rebellious republic; map; photo (M)
news.title: Troops Try to Regain Footing in Chechnya After Rebel Strikes

news.abstract: Vice Pres Al Gore presides during presidential primary campaign over unusual United Nations Security Council session on AIDS crisis in Africa; says United States will increase spending by $150 million to combat infectious diseases in poorest nations; World Bank president, James D Wolfensohn, warns epidemic is more effective than war in destabilizing nations; experts say at least 70 percent of over 33 million people infected with AIDS virus are African; Sec Gen Kofi Annan cites need to smash wall of silence and stigma surrounding AIDS; US Amb Richard C Holbrooke organized debate; graphs of causes of death and declining life expectancy in Africa; photo (M)
news.title: Gore Presides Over Rare Security Council Debate on AIDS

news.abstract: Pres Clinton plans $1.28 billion emergency aid program to help Colombia fight growing drug trade and to prop up its democracy over next two years; much of money would be spent on military hardware to upgrade Colombian forces battling narcotics traders, many of whom are aligned with antigovernment rebels; funds would also be used to help strengthen justice system and aid people displaced by civil war (M)
news.title: Clinton to Offer Aid in Colombia Drug War

news.abstract: Opposition groups score Ecuador Pres Jamil Mahuad's bid to solve economic crisis by adopting United States dollar as new currency; warn of 'massive impoverishment;' threaten to paralyze nation until he resigns; Mahaud also has asked cabinet to resign (M)
news.title: Foes Fight Ecuador's Leader on Dollar Plan

news.abstract: Prime Min Ehud Barak returns to Israel and reports that peace talks with Syria have reached 'decisive stage' in which both sides will have to make difficult decisions, television interview; sees 'certain fissures' in Syrian rigidity but is not reading too much into them; dismisses concerns that Pres Hafez al-Assad shows disrespect by sending Foreign Min Farouk al-Shara, and declines to make issue of whether or not he and Shara shake hands; says no in-depth talks on borders have taken place and Israelis have made no political commitment on withdrawal from Golan Heights (S)
news.title: Barak Says Talks With Syria Have Reached Critical Juncture

news.abstract: Mexico City Journal on confusion of Mexico City street names; photo; map; developers each year carve out some 1,500 new streets, another 300 are renamed because honorees have fallen out of favor; 1998 survey found 80,000 blocks lack signs, thousands of avenues have no official name, and others carry names of politicians in ill repute; favorite names are repeated dozens of times; current review appears prompted by 17 streets named for Carlos Salinas de Gortari, former president associated with plunder of public treasury (M)
news.title: Mexico City Journal; Can't Find Juarez Street? There Are Hundreds!

news.abstract: Karlheinz Schreiber, millionaire German arms broker, is fighting extradition from Canada to testify in corruption investigation of former Chancellor Helmut Kohl; Schreiber acknowledges handing envelope stuffed with one million marks to Christian Democratic emissaries in Swiss restaurant in 1991, but says it was campaign money, not bribe; photo (M)
news.title: A German-Canadian Fights Extradition: He's a Key Figure in Kohl Case

news.abstract: Russian commanders in Shali, Chechnya, provide first on-the-scene account of fighting that has alarmed authorities in Moscow and prompted close review of strategy in breakaway province; photos; map; suprise offensive by Chechens in Shali and Argun recounted; Defense Min Igor Sergeyev says situation has radically changed (M)
news.title: Chechen Rebels Swim in Friendly Waters to Nip Russians

news.abstract: Streak of obstinacy that helped Helmut Kohl unify Germany and persuade his countrymen to abandon their beloved mark for euro now appears to be unhinging his Christian Democratic party and unraveling Kohl's reputation; Kohl has opened devastating party divisions by admitting he accepted over $1 million in secret payments to party but refusing to reveal donors' names or leave politics in face of criminal investigation; Wolfgang Schauble, current party leader and Kohl protege, now admits to taking $52,000 in cash in 1994 from Karlheinz Schreiber, arms broker now fighting extradition from Canada; Schauble says he passed money along to party treasurer Brigitte Baumeister; Schauble has until now tried to distance himself from affair, but neither he nor Kohl appear to have entirely grasped gravity of scandal; photo (M)
news.title: Kohl, a Stubborn Statesman, May Be Wrecking His Party

news.abstract: Lee Keating, former supervisor at Shelburne School for Boys, reformatory in Nova Scotia, is among 84 former employees who object to decision of Nova Scota provincial government to accept largely on face value charges of former residents of school that they were physically or sexually abused by staff members, and to pay them from $25 million compensation fund for victims; one former employee was convicted of sex abuse in 1993, after which many suits were filed by former residents against virtually entire staff; Keating and others say they are victims of witch hunt; photos; map (M)
news.title: Shelburne Journal; Tales of Sex, Violence and Greed in a Small Town

news.abstract: Henry Pleasants, 89, music critic, author and historian of the singing voice, died in a London hospital Jan. 4 after suffering a ruptured aorta. He had lived in London for more than 30 years.
news.title: OBITUARY : Henry Pleasants, 89, Music Critic, Dies

news.abstract: Nelson Mandela, former South African president, will attend Security Council debate on worsening political and economic situation in Burundi; Mandela is new international mediator for Burundi; at center of debate is Burundi's 'regroupment' policy under which Tutsi-led government of Pres Pierre Buyoya has forcibly resettled 300,000 mostly ethnic Hutus in dozens of spartan camps (M)
news.title: Mandela's Next Job: Trying to Cool One of Africa's Hottest Spots

news.abstract: MILAN—  As dress codes in the workplace continue to ease up, the race is on to find a comfortable alternative to the conventional suit and a new generation of designers see sportswear as the best solution.
news.title: Luxury Sportswear Casually Trumps the Suit

news.abstract: British government ends its ban on openly gay men and women serving in armed forces, following European court ruling that Britain could no longer keep the exclusion; this ends Britain's decades-old practice of subjecting gays in military to intrusive investigations and dishonorable discharges; change brings Britain into line with almost all other NATO nations, which allow openly gay men and lesbians to serve in their armed forces; United States, with its 'don't ask, don't tell' policy, is at variance with trend; Britain's about-face became inevitable after European Court of Human Rights unanimously ruled last September in favor of four former servicemen and servicewomen who were discharged in mid-1990's because of their homosexuality; photo (M)
news.title: British, Under European Ruling, End Ban on Openly Gay Soldiers

news.abstract: Security Council is confronting issue of how new wars are demanding new definitions and new policies if millions of people they have made homeless are to survive; refugee experts say 20 million or more people have abandoned their houses, driven forcibly by governments and guerrilla armies or voluntarily in search of safety; because they remain in their own countires, they fall outside purview of organization's high commissioner for refugees; high commissioner, Sadako Ogata, has pushed hard to include internally displaced within her organization's reach, thereby making them eligible for international aid; United States representative, Richard C Holbrooke, has urged council to rethink how refugee organization could be retooled to meet crisis that exists around world (M)
news.title: U.N. Studies How Refugees Qualify to Get Assistance

news.abstract: Russian military leaders say they have again taken control of Argun from Chechen rebels, but soldiers moving through are nervous about snipers and clearly do not think all danger has passed; Argun has become conspicuous example of how hard it may be for Russia to keep what it has taken; some officers doubt that Argun, first taken by Russians in early December, would ever be totally secure; Russian commandant of town, Col Vladimir N Kushnaryov, is gunned down after his armored column is surrounded; photo; map (M)
news.title: Russia Takes Chechen Town, but Can It Keep It?

news.abstract: ASIA    INDIA: EX-STATE CHIEF CLEARED  Jayalalitha Jayaram, the former actress and onetime chief minister of the state of Tamil Nadu, won an important victory in a criminal case when charges against her in a reportedly crooked land deal were dropped. The same state court also upheld an earlier ruling that absolved her of guilt in a reported coal-importing scam. Two other charges against her are still pending.   Barry Bearak (NYT)    MALAYSIA: CRACKDOWN CONTINUES  The government extended a crackdown on opposition figures, arresting another top political leader and charging two people with sedition. The latest arrest, the fifth since Wednesday, was that of Mohamed Ezam Mohamed Nor, left, a senior leader of the National Justice Party, which supports the jailed politician Anwar Ibrahim. Mr. Mohamed Ezam said he was being charged under the Official Secrets Act.   (AP)
news.title: WORLD BRIEFING

news.abstract: Gloria Trevi, pop star in Mexico, and her manager, Sergio Andrade Sanchez, are arrested in Brazil on Mexican charges of corrupting minors; Andrade is accused of forcing sex on young girls who were among his teenage protegees; he and Trevi dropped from view over year ago; scandal has exposed underside of entertainment world filled with freewheeling sex, where Andrade had gained mesmerizing power of cult leader with young girls who hoped for stardom; charges against him and Trevi were first brought by parents of young girl who claim Andrade kidnapped her and fathered her baby by force; photos (M)
news.title: Mexican Star in Sex Case Is Arrested in Rio

news.abstract: Buckingham Palace announces that it is withdrawing royal warrant awarded by Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, to Harrods, London department store that is owned by Mohamed al-Fayed; Fayed, Egyptian-born businessman, has become irritant to royal family over last two years by persistently theorizing that car crash that took lives of his son and Princess Diana was conspiracy planned by British secret security forces to keep Diana from marrying his son; photo (M)
news.title: Harrods Loses Prince Philip's Seal of Approval

news.abstract: Russian troops in Chechnya are accompanied by Orthodox Church chaplains who offer comfort and help with personal problems; one priest, Father Safrony, sees himself as heir to pre-Soviet tradition, and says he tells soldiers they are defending sacred Russian land; photos; map (M)
news.title: New on the Russian Front Lines: Army Chaplains

news.abstract: LONDON—  Glaxo Wellcome PLC and SmithKline Beecham PLC, whose botched merger attempt two years ago stood out as one of the costliest failures of the 1990s merger boom, said Friday that they had revived talks toward a combination that would create the world's largest pharmaceutical company.
news.title: Glaxo and SmithKline Try Again After Costly Failure : Drug Giants Talk Merger

news.abstract: Serbs in Kursumlija, ten miles from Kosovo border, complain of attacks and land mines by Kosovo Albanians, former members of separatist Kosovo Liberation Army; photo; map; Serbian police report at least 16 attacks on officers and villagers since June (M)
news.title: Kursumlija Journal; Serbs at Border Complain of Attacks From Kosovo

news.abstract: US finds few international supporters for proposal that any global pact on military service age allow volunteers younger than 18 to fight for their country; US allows volunteer enlistments at age 17 with parental consent; Britain recruits at age 16; human rights campaigners seek minimum age of 18 (S)
news.title: U.S. Fights Tide on a Move to Raise the Military Service Age

news.abstract: International war crimes tribunal in The Hague convicts and sentences five Bosnian Croat militiamen for taking part in massacre of more than 100 Muslims in Bosnian village of Ahmici, in April 1993; court, in largest case to date, finds that killings of Muslims, including children, burned alive in their homes were part of organized terror campaign; five get sentences of six to 25 years (S)
news.title: War Crimes Court Convicts 5 Bosnian Croats in '93 Massacre

news.abstract: Canadian hospitals are overflowing with patients, reflecting strains on nation's state-run health system and causing many hundreds of Canadians to cross border for treatment in US; hospitals are turning away ambulances this winter, and patients are often stacked up in hallways; photo; map; government has both closed door to foreign doctors and cut number of spaces in medical schools; 6,000 nurses and at least 1,000 doctors have moved to US in recent years; hospitals have long waiting lists even for heart surgery and cancer treatmentand critical CAT scans (M)
news.title: Full Hospitals Make Canadians Wait and Look South

news.abstract: Ecuadoran Pres Jamil Mahuad, facing resignation or ouster in recent weeks, may have bought reprieve with surprise move to replace local currency with US dollar, in hopes of stabilizing economy after months of crisis; photo of demonstrator (M)
news.title: Dollar May Buy a Reprieve in Ecuador

news.abstract: France presses UN to find ways to make AIDS drugs available to poor nations; envoy Alain Dejammeet makes proposals at Security Council meeting on AIDS crisis in Africa (S)
news.title: France Presses the U.N. to Help Poor Nations Get AIDS Drugs

news.abstract: Chilean presidential campaign between Ricardo Lagos, austere Socialist, and Joaquin Lavin, ebullient conservative who began career under Gen Augusto Pinochet, explained; photos (M)
news.title: In Chile's Vote Today, Candidates Converge in Center

news.abstract: Ethnic Serbs who fled Croatia during strife of last decade find they are unable to return because towns like Knin, center of Serb resistance, are almost entirely repopulated by Croats from neighboring Bosnia, themselves refugees from war; Pres Franjo Tudjman had promised to help refugees return, as part of Dayton peace accords, but local housing authorities ignore requests, using red tape to block Serb' return and preventing them from repairing homes; photos (M)
news.title: For Serbs in Croatia, a Pledge Unkept

news.abstract: Clinton administration officials say Vladimir V Putin, Russia's acting president, appears to be a modern decision maker who knows how to make things happen, but they are unsure whether his political instincts match that style of action; their initial take on Putin is that he sees Russia's future as a fairly democratic one, with a market economy of some kind and participation in the world community; photo (M)
news.title: U.S. Officials Pore Over Putin's Resume

news.abstract: Estrongo Nachama, chief cantor of Berlin Jewish community and the man who did as much as anyone to revive Jewish life in the city after Hitler destroyed it, dies at age 81; photo (M)
news.title: Estrongo Nachama, 81, Dies; Chief Cantor of Berlin's Jews

news.abstract: Nelson Mandela, former president of South Africa, begins his duties as mediator for conflict in Burundi with an extraordinary attack on the nation's warring leaders--seated in a long row in front of him--for failing their people and shaming Africa; outlines major points of contention with business-like precision and suggests that he hopes to bring regional and even world leaders into the effort to find peace for Burundi; photo (M)
news.title: Warring Sides in Burundi Get a Scolding From Mandela

news.abstract: CIA reportedly informs senior Clinton administration officials that Iran may now be able to make a nuclear weapons, touching off a sharp debate about Iran's nuclear capacity and the CIA's ability to monitor it; evaluation is apparently not based on evidence that Iran's indigenous efforts to build a bomb have achieved a breakthrough, but rather on fact that US cannot track with great certainty the increased efforts by Iran to acquire nuclear materials technology in international black market; US has made little headway with efforts to weaken longstanding strategic relationship between Iran and Russia, which is still brimming with stockpiles of nuclear fuel and weapons related technology and has long sold sensitive nuclear and missile technology to Iran; photo (M)
news.title: C.I.A. Tells Clinton An Iranian A-Bomb Can't Be Ruled Out

news.abstract: Prime Min Ehud Barak postpones an Israeli withdrawal West Bank until after his meeting with Syrian officials in Washington; Palestinians condemn action; photo (M)
news.title: Barak Delays 3rd West Bank Transfer, Angering Palestinians

news.abstract: Bomb explodes in garbage can in northern Israeli town of Hadera, injuring 20 people; police suspect members of Islamic Holy War (S)
news.title: Bomb Explodes in Northern Israeli Town

news.abstract: Man-in-the-News biographical sketch of Chile's President-elect Ricardo Lagos; economist and lawyer is Socialist and longtime political moderate; photo (M)
news.title: MAN IN THE NEWS: Ricardo Lagos Escobar; A Chilean Socialist in the Clinton-Blair Mold

news.abstract: UN Sec Gen Kofi Annan selects Rolf Ekeus, Swedish arms-control expert who found and destroyed large quantities of Iraqi weapons after 1991 Persian Gulf war, to head new commission created to finish job more than year after arms monitoring broke down; action follows failure of Security Council to meet deadline to make nomination and is seen as challenge to Iraq's supporters on council, particularly Russia, China and France, to veto choice; Iraq, longtime critic of Ekeus, ridicules selection; Russia formally registers objection, throwing nomination in doubt; council delegations express concern that Iraq's friends could engage in filibuster on nomination, stalling action on new inspection system and indefinitely postponing any resolution of Iraq crisis (M)
news.title: Annan Picks Ex-Arms Inspector To Head Iraq Monitoring Panel

news.abstract: Imprisoned Kurdish rebel leader Abdullah Ocalan seeks role in incipient national dialogue about how Turkey should deal with its Kurdish minority following decision by government to suspend his execution; Prime Min Bulent Ecevit says Ocalan can have no role in dialogue; says he is using prison as pulpit to dictate to Turkish government (S)
news.title: Rebel Leader Wants a Voice In Turkey's National Dialogue

news.abstract: Agua Prieta, gritty Mexican desert town that shares border with Douglas, Ariz, has become busiest border crossing area along 2,000-mile dividing line between US and Mexico for undocumented Mexican immigrants; surge has overwhelmed 26-mile section of border, and Border Patrol has run out of detention space; 14,664 undocumented migrants have been detained since beginning of year, or nearly twice as many as during corresponding period in 1999; photo; chart; map (M)
news.title: Agua Prieta Journal; Boom Turns Border to Speed Bump

news.abstract: Some of world's largest Christian denominations boycott ceremony in Rome celebrating start of Roman Catholic Holy Year because Pope John Paul II is using occasion to highlight importance of indulgences, practice that helped set off Protestant Reformation; gathering at St Paul's Outside the Walls Basilica is one of largest interfaith gatherings since Second Vatican Council, and it is attended by representatives from 22 Christian churches; pope delivers homily on need to repent for divisions within Christianity; photo (M)
news.title: The Pope Opens a Door, but Not All Christians Feel Welcome

news.abstract: Is an Ivy League education — which today can cost dollars 120,000 or more — the best investment in terms of future earning capacity? The answer is not as clear as it once appeared.
news.title: AMERICAN TOPICS : Ivy League Isn't Top Path to Riches

news.abstract: Russian forces battle way toward center of Grozny as struggle for control of Chechnya's capital enters even fiercer phase; seek to fracture rebel defenses and seize heart of city; maps (M)
news.title: In Onslaught, Russian Force Enters Grozny

news.abstract: Syrians are confident that peace agreement with Israel will be reached eventually, despite cancellation of second round of talks in Shepherdstown, West Va, because of lack of progress (M)
news.title: Syrians Shrug Off Lapse in Peace Talks

news.abstract: Serbian government of Pres Slobodan Milosevic denies role in assassination of Zeljko Raznatovic, notorious Serb paramilitary leader known as Arkan; says Arkan was criminal and was killed by Montenegrin mafia seeking to take over Belgrade; says gunman wounded in attack has been identified as Dusan Gavric, member of Raznatovic's paramilitary group since 1993; promises new developments soon in long-standing police investigation of 1997 gangland-style shooting of Zoran Todorovic, politician who was close associate of Milosevic's wife, Mirjana Markovic, and senior official of her Yugoslav United Left party; his death has also been blamed on Milosevic government (M)
news.title: Milosevic Government Denies Role in Killing of Serbian Warlord

news.abstract: British government says Royal Ulster Constabulary, militaristic police force of Northern Ireland, will be reduced in size, its membership broadened to better reflect population of province and its politically charged name retired; Northern Ireland Secretary Peter Mandelson tells boisterous session of Parliament that changes are needed to produce modern, effective police service that draws support and strength from all parts of community (M)
news.title: Britain to Shrink the Ulster Constabulary and Broaden Its Ranks

news.abstract: News analysis of decision by Russian Pres Vladimir Putin to cut deal with Communists in legislature, leaving pro-democratic factions out of important positions; his willingness to forsake ideological allies and embrace ideological enemies seems aimed at consolidating his power; photo (M)
news.title: Moscow's Strange Bedfellows

news.abstract: Clinton Clinton administration warns against allowing government of Saddam Hussein to exercise veto power over UN decisions on how to resume arms inspections in Iraq; criticizes members of Security Council blocking Sec Gen Kofi Annan's appointment of Rolf Ekeus as head of new disarmament commission for Iraq; Russia, France and China have objected to return of Ekeus, executive chairman of first disarmament commission for Iraq from creation after Persian Gulf war in 1991 until 1997; say Ekeus, who cooperated closely with US, is unacceptable to Iraqis (S)
news.title: U.S. Criticizes U.N. Backers Of Iraq's 'No' To Appointee

news.abstract: Lt Gen Gennadi Troshev, deputy commander of Russian forces in northern Caucasus, says military plans to end campaign in Chechnya by February 26, exactly month before presidential election; statement underscores political imperative of bringing war in breakaway province to early close; Russian forces press assault on Grozny, Chechen capital; are reportadly advancing slowly against smaller but determined group of rebels, who have mined streets and are using small mobile bands of fighters; maps (M)
news.title: Russian Aim: Wind Up the War in Chechnya Before Election

news.abstract: National Autonomous University of Mexico, once proud symbol of nation's publicly financed education for masses, is crippled by strike that began in April 1999 as limited student protest seeking to preserve free tuition and open admissions but has spun out of control of administrators, Pres Ernesto Zedillo and even broad-based student organization that initiated it; has suffered losses in students, research, finances and especially academic stature that it will probably never recoup; strike has dragged on because tough, anarchic leftist movement that took control of revolt has run headlong into new world and new Mexico, where shrinking public spending can no longer promote social mobility through huge and generous institutions like national university; photo (M)
news.title: University, Mexico's Pride, Is Ravaged by Strike

news.abstract: Palestinian leader Yasir Arafat, with Syrian-Israeli talks in abeyance, has full attention of Pres Clinton and State Sec Madeleine K Albright, capped by lunch with Albright at her Georgetown house (S)
news.title: Spotlight on Arafat, Capital's Lone Mideast Player

news.abstract: After four months of war in north Caucasus, serious doubts have been raised about Russian military's official death count--by media, by experts, by soldiers' families and by Russian soldiers themselves, who have taken to yelling out higher death tolls to reporters visiting sites of recent battles (M)
news.title: Many Doubt Official Chechnya Toll

news.abstract: Excerpts from Sen Jesse Helms's speech to United Nations Security Council (M)
news.title: In the Words of Helms: 'A Lack of Gratitude'

news.abstract: Head of China's central bank describes renewed efforts to turn China's giant state banks and ailing state enterprises into sound commercial operations, able to withstand the competitive pressures that are certain to follow China's entry into World Trade Orgn; Dai Xianglong, head of People's Bank of China, speaking at his annual news conference, also pledges a smooth growth in money supply and a stable exchange rate (M)
news.title: China to End Bank Secrecy In Effort Against Corruption

news.abstract: Sen Jesse Helms visits United Nations Security Council offering 'hand of friendship' but delivers sort of clenched-fist message that has made him symbol of right-wing hostility toward United Nations; Helms, North Carolina Republican and most powerful Congressional voice in foreign policy as chmn of Senate Foreign Relations Committee, contends Congress has right to dictate conditions for payment of American debts to organization; warns UN to keep its 'utopian' visions away from American sovereignty (M)
news.title: Helms, in Visit To U.N., Offers Harsh Message

news.abstract: Isabel Allende, daughter of Salvador Allende, celebrates her 55th birthday and election of Ricardo Lagos, first Socialist to win power in Chile since her father died in military coup in 1973; interview; photo; she predicts subdued reaction if former dictator Augusto Pinochet returns from Britain (S)
news.title: Allende's Daughter Sees a Circle Closing

news.abstract: Huge smuggling scandal under investigation in China involves dozens of Communist party, police and banking officials, wife of Beijing's powerful party chief, virtually entire customs department of major seaport of Xiamen and flamboyant corporate figure, Lai Changxing, who has vanished; sprawling syndicate smuggled billions of dollars worth of cars, oil and industrial materials through Xiamen in 1990's; case embarrasses Jiang Zemin's government and suggests critical weaknesses in Communist party and its ability to rule vast country; only hints have been published in official press, but Beijing party officials confirm that Xiamen deputy mayor Lan Fu and wife have fled country; Lin Youfang, wife of Beijing official Jia Qinglin, is detained (M)
news.title: BIG SMUGGLING RING WITH A WIDE REACH SCANDALIZES CHINA

news.abstract: Crisis in Germany's Christian Democratic party, which has served to marginalize extreme-right movement, may benefit rightist fringe parties; concern is that ethics accusations against former Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his party could shake relatively shallow roots of German democracy (M)
news.title: Gain for Germany's Far Right Feared

news.abstract: Negotiators in Geneva agree on new international accord barring use of child soldiers in war; US drops opposition to setting 18 as minimum age for sending soldiers into combat, after months of pressure from Pentagon to keep age 17 as option; Joint Chiefs of Staff accept compromise allowing recruitment and training of 17-year-olds as long as 'all feasible measures' are taken to keep them out of combat; new minimum will have little real effect on US military (M)
news.title: Agreement Bars Using Children as Soldiers

news.abstract: Two car bombs explode in Madrid, killing army officer, Pedro Antonio Blanco Garcia, and injuring other people; government blames Basque separatist group ETA (S)
news.title: 2 Bombs, One Lethal, Explode in Madrid; Spain Blames Basques

news.abstract: Ecuadoran Vice president Gustavo Noboa Bejarno assumes control of government after dissident military officers and Indian groups overthrow elected president Jamil Mahuad; takes office after armed forces chief Gen Carlos Mendoza dissolves three-man junta that briefly led government; Mendoza says move is aimed at preventing international isolation of Ecuador; threats by US and Latin American countries to impose sanctions if constitutional rule was not preserved noted; Noboa becomes sixth chief of state in four years; says he has support of armed forces and national police; Mahuad condemns coup but acknowledges Noboa's authority; coup is Latin America's first overthrow of sitting civilian president in more than decade; comes amid Ecuador's worst economic crisis in more than 70 years; economy contracted by 7.5 percent in 1999, and inflation was more than 80 percent for second consecutive year--worst economic performance in Latin America; country defaulted on half of its $13 billion foreign debt in September 1999; map; photo (M)
news.title: Ecuador Coup Shifts Control To No. 2 Man

news.abstract: Taiwan's Nationalist Party, which has governed for more than 50 years, is in danger of losing presidency in upcoming elections amid allegations of corruption; candidate, Vice Pres Lien Chan, is trailing rivals in close race to succeed Lee Teng-hui, and prospect of victory by opposition has rattled political establishment; has forced Nationalists to make significant concessions that could permanently alter power structure in Taiwan, regardless of who wins election on March 18; photos; maps (M)
news.title: An Embarrassment of Riches Hurts Taiwan's Ruling Party

news.abstract: Ruhiyyih Rabbani, who became pre-eminent member of Bahai faith after death of her husband, last official leader of faith, dies at 89; photo (M)
news.title: No Headline

news.abstract: Guatemalan police arrest father and son military officers, retired Col Byron Disrael Lima Estrada and Capt Byron Lima Oliva for murder in 1998 death of Roman Catholic bishop and vigorous human rights advocate Juan Jose Gerardi; arrests make good on pledge by new Pres Alfonso Portillo to bring killers to justice and is victory for human rights groups in Guatemala, which conducted own investigation and have long pointed to Limas as suspects (M)
news.title: Arrests in Bishop's Killing Follow Guatemalan Pledge

news.abstract: Eleven members of Rylstone, England, chapter of Women's Institute, aged 45 to 66, provoke wide-eyed interest by posing nude and substituting photos on their annual calendar, instead of usual images of watery sunsets and hiking paths bursting with buttercups, in ploy to raise money for leukemia research; wholesome rural service organization, better known for 'jam and Jerusalem'--home of bottled preserves from English country kitchens and Blake poem enshrining 'England's green and pleasant land'--raises $550,000 from calender sales, surpassing projected $2,000, and even wins unexpected praise from thousands of middle-aged women who say calender has restored their own flagging self-esteem; photos; map (M)
news.title: Rylstone Journal; The Stately 'Calendar Girls' Dressed So Simply in Pearls

news.abstract: News analysis of UN Amb Richard C Holbrooke's success in giving world body high degree of visibility among Washington's movers and shakers; Holbrooke's carefully orchestrated meetings and nonstop hospitality to influential members of Congress may have made UN safe again for American politicians (M)
news.title: Beltway on Display: American Politics at the U.N.

news.abstract: Pres Ezer Weizman of Israel defiantly rebuts calls by political allies and opponents, as well as news media, to resign or step down temporarily while police pursue criminal investigation of his receipt of hundreds of thousands of dollars from French businessman, Edouard Saroussi; denies in televised address that he broke law or otherwise engaged in wrongdoing; says he will issue statement about facts of affair when investigation is over (M)
news.title: President Of Israel Faces Accusations With Defiance

news.abstract: Armed rebels from Burmese insurgent group called God's Army reportedly cross border into Thailand and seize local hospital, taking as many as 200 people hostage and demanding medical care for their wounded (S)
news.title: Burmese Rebels Seize Hostages in Thailand

news.abstract: Approximately one million people march in Madrid, Spain, in protest against Basque separatist group ETA, suspected in two car bombings in city in which army officer died; march is led by Prime Min Jose Maria Aznar and three former prime ministers and caps weekend of nationwide protests; bombings appear to reignite separatist violence after 18-month lull; photo (M)
news.title: A Million Protesters in Spain Denounce Terrorism's Return

news.abstract: Decision by Japan's Aum Shinrikyo sect to denounce spiritual leader Shoko Asahara for role in 1991 nerve gas attack against Tokyo subway system that killed 12 people, and to change its name to Aleph appears to have raised more fears than it calmed; organizations that use name Aleph have been flooded with telephone calls from people concerned that they are associated with sect; photo (M)
news.title: Japan Sect's Name Change Brings Confusion and Fear

news.abstract: Russia's first deputy prime minister Mikhail Kasaynov acknowledges that Kremlin underestimated cost of Chechen war and spent 50 percent more in 1999 than initially planned; says government budgeted $125 million, but instead spent $178 million; soaring economic and military costs reflect intensity of fighting in Chechnya and inability of Russian forces to bring conflict to early close; are expected to sharpen Western debate over providing credits and other forms of economic assistance to Russia; photos (M)
news.title: Russia Says Cost of Chechen War Far Exceeds Estimate

news.abstract: FRANKFURT—  Germany's scandal-shaken conservative party, which Monday confirmed that it cannot account for more than 12 million Deutsche marks in political funds, said that it was mired in an "existential trial" and would begin a national campaign to win back public trust.
news.title: Party Audit Finds Shortfall in Kohl Era

news.abstract: Supreme Court clears way for US to send Rwandan church leader, Elizaphan Ntakirutimana, to war crimes tribunal, where he is wanted on charges of abetting genocide in 1994 for allowing armed Hutus to enter his church and kill hundreds of Tutsis who sought refuge there; he was arrested in Texas in 1996 by federal marshals acting under agreement between US and war crimes tribunals for Balkans and Rwanda, but judge ruled agreement, subsequently enacted into law later in year, unconstitutional and ordered him released in 1997 (M)
news.title: Way Clear for U.S. to Deliver Rwanda War Crimes Suspect

news.abstract: Audit of Germany's Christian Democratic Union shows more than $6.3 million in illicit contributions under former Chancellor Helmut Kohl, suggesting system of secret financing far greater than previously ackowledged; audit by Ernst & Young provides no clues to sources of payments to Kohl's party that he has refused to reveal; shows $1 million Kohl admits receiving from 1993 to 1998 followed earlier and much larger payments (M)
news.title: Audit Traces Illegal Funds In Kohl Party

news.abstract: Interview with Amos Gitai, one of Israel's few internationally acclaimed filmmakers, about movie Kippur--his deeply personal film about warfare on Golan Heights during 1973 Arab-Israeli war; photo; map (M)
news.title: Nafah Journal; Now Shooting on Golan: A War Movie

news.abstract: Harkat ul-Mujahedeen, militant group believed responsible for hijacking of Indian Airlines jet in December, emerged in early 1990's as movement dedicated to Kashmir operations against Indian troops and civilian targets; US believes group is supported by Pakistani intelligence service and is extending its influence as militant Islamic political parties gain power in Pakistan; State Department's 1999 report on global terrorism linked group, under Fazlur Rehman Khalil, to Osama bin Laden; group operated terrorist training camps in Afghanistan and suffered casualties during US missile strikes aganst bin Laden in 1998; Khalil warned of revenge; Pakistani leader Gen Pervez Musharraf has turned down request by three senior Clinton administration officials to shut down group; officials were in Pakistan to assess prospects for stopover by Pres Clinton during trip to region in March (M)
news.title: Pakistanis Lost Control Of Militants, U.S. Hints

news.abstract: EUROPE    BRITAIN: MARRIAGE AND DIVORCE -- A high-ranking Church of England committee recommended that the divorced be permitted to remarry even if former spouses are still living. The move would formalize what is now common practice and would pave the way for the Prince of Wales to marry his longtime companion, Camilla Parker Bowles, left, an event previously seen as impossible for a future supreme governor of the church. To take effect, the recommendation must be adopted by the church Synod, which meets next year.   Warren Hoge (NYT)    BRITAIN: BELGIUM'S PINOCHET PLEA -- Belgium joined six rights groups in a move in the High Court to keep Britain from letting Gen. Augusto Pinochet, 84, return home to Chile. Belgium is seeking an order blocking his departure until he is examined by Belgian doctors. Home Secretary Jack Straw has refused to make public a report by four British doctors that found the former dictator medically unfit to stand trial in Spain on torture charges. Brussels has filed an extradition bid in behalf of Chileans living in Belgium.   Warren Hoge (NYT)
news.title: WORLD BRIEFING

news.abstract: Colombian Pres Andres Pastrana visits Washington and begins campaigning for Congress to approve more than billion dollars in emergency aid not tied to his military's actions on human rights; meets with Pres Clinton and says in interview that, while his government is committed to improving rights record, efforts will not be helped by further US pressure; photo (M)
news.title: Colombian Asks Congress for Aid Not Tied to Human Rights

news.abstract: Turkey is in shock over discovery of dozens of savagely tortured bodies beneath hide-outs of religious terror group Hizbullah or Party of God, which aims to overthrow secular state and establish Islamic republic; outrage and grief focuses on Konca Kuris, writer often described as Muslim feminist; she was kidnapped in front of her home in July 1998 and not seen again until burned, disfigured body was exhumed from shallow grave in Koyna, one of 33 found so far at Hizbullah properties; photo; videotapes of her torture also reported found; most of other victims apparently were Kurdish businessmen from war-torn provinces in southeast (S)
news.title: Turkish Terror Victim Espoused a Tolerant Islam

news.abstract: GENEVA—  Switzerland is confronting the largest dirty money investigation in its history after disclosures that dollars 654 million has been found in accounts in the names of the former Nigerian dictator Sani Abacha, his family and associates.
news.title: Swiss Freeze A Dictator's Giant Cache

news.abstract: US investigators have uncovered what they believe are links between Algerians who have been charged with plotting terrorist attack in US and Osama bin Laden, exiled Saudi accused of bombing two US Embassies in East Africa; authorities in Senegal recently arrested Mohambedou Ould Slahi; US investigators believe that he directed Algerian group in Canada in its efforts to enter US and carry out bomb plot late last year; say Slahi is brother-in-law of one of bin Laden's key lieutenants, but they refuse to identify him; bomb plot was foiled when border agents in Port Angeles, Wash, on Dec 14 arrested Ahmed Ressam, Algerian who was driving car loaded with explosives (M)
news.title: EVIDENCE IS SEEN LINKING BIN LADEN TO ALGERIAN GROUP

news.abstract: Young Syrian entrepreneurs like Hashem Akkad, legislator and businessman, are eager to catch up with their contemporaries in other Arab countries; say Pres Hafez al-Assad's economic policies are built on socialism and cronyism and should be liberalized; photo (M)
news.title: Syria Businessmen Yearn for Reforms

news.abstract: United Nations Security Council, laying groundwork for eventual United Nations peacekeeping operation in Congo, urges African nations involved in war to put into effect peace accord they negotiated last summer (M)
news.title: U.N. Urges End to Congo Cease-Fire Impasse

news.abstract: Mexican government asserts that its soldiers and police seized far more drugs in 1999 than in previous years, partly as result of increased spending on high-tech gadgetry, aircraft and naval vessels deployed in narcotics war (M)
news.title: Mexico Gives Itself High Marks for Last Year's Anti-Drug Effort

news.abstract: While Syria and Israel have been discussing an end to their 52-year state of war, many Syrian businessmen fear they would not reap any economic dividends of peace, despite its promise of access to Western markets and investment.     Instead, these restless executives, fully equipped with luxury cars, marble-floored offices, satellite dishes, tailored suits and high-end computers, say that the question of whether they will do business with Israelis after a peace treaty is irrelevant.
news.title: Syrians Not Counting On Peace Dividends

news.abstract: Germany ends decade of turbulent debate over how to commemorate Holocaust in its new capital by dedicating a vast site beside the Brandenburg Gate for a memorial designed by New York architect Peter Eisenman; most of German government stands in icy winds beneath new billboards announcing 'Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe' as Wolfgang Thierse, speaker of Parliament, explains that honor has to be accorded to six million Jewish dead 'in the heart of our capital city'; construction will begin next year on 4.9-acre site; field of more than 2,000 stone pillars of varying dimensions will be flanked by 'documentation center' whose precise role remains unclear; resistant to the last, Eberhard Diepgen, Berlin's Christian Democratic mayor, snubs ceremony; Germany, to complete its formal remembrance of Holocaust, on 55th anniversary of liberation of Auschwitz, invites Elie Wiesel, Nobel Peace laureate, to address lower house of Parliament; photos (L)
news.title: Wiesel Urges Germany to Ask Forgiveness

news.abstract: Clinton adm issues public warning to Pakistan that it could be branded a state sponsor of terrorism--ending any hope for a resumption of large-scale American aid--if Pakistani Army continues to support terrorists blamed for hijacking of Indian Airlines jet last month (S)
news.title: U.S. Warns Pakistan It May Be Branded a Sponsor of Terrorism

news.abstract: Delegates at global biosafety conference in Montreal debate 'precautionary principle' as they strive to negotiate world's first treaty regulating trade in genetically modified products; negotiators ask whether a nation must have scientific proof before it can ban a genetically engineered crop or animal, or can it act even in absence of scientific certainty (M)
news.title: Talks on Biotech Food Turn on a Safety Principle

news.abstract: Governing coalition in Japan, in move that sets stage for major political showdown, pushes through bill to eliminate 20 seats from 500-seat lower house of Parliament; all 20 are from 200 seats chosen by proportional representation, and opposition politicians say move would favor Prime Min Keizo Obuchi's coalition (S)
news.title: Bill Widens Gulf in Japan

news.abstract: Leaders of three Russian political parties agree to end their boycott of Russian Parliament on Feb 9, thereby avoiding an open-ended confrontation with acting president, Vladimir V Putin, and his parliamentary allies (M)
news.title: Russians Agree to End Parliament Walkout

news.abstract: DAVOS, Switzerland—  When the talk is of digital convergence or financial markets, the optimism, even euphoria, is palpable throughout the conference halls and corridors of the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum now under way in this chic Alpine ski resort.
news.title: Global Elite Are Fretting On Response To Backlash

news.abstract: Dominique Strauss-Kahn, a former French finance minister, is being investigated in connection with $29,000 that his secretary, Evelyne Duval, received from the oil company Elf Aquitaine in 1993 (M)
news.title: Ex-Official In France Again Faces Investigation

news.abstract: South Africa's Parliament passes far-reaching bill explicity outlawing discrimination on basis of race, ethnicity and sex; bill would also ban discrimination against homosexuals, pregnant women and the disabled and bar malicious use of derogatory labels for blacks and other people of color; protection extended in earlier draft to poor people, foreigners and people infected with HIV is removed after protests from business leaders and others (M)
news.title: South Africa Codifies Ban on Bias In Constitution

news.abstract: EUROPE    THE HAGUE: WAR CRIMES CASE OPENS -- Mitar Vasiljevic, a Bosnian Serb accused of killing 135 Muslim men, women and children by locking them inside two houses in Visigrad in June 1992 and setting the buildings on fire, made his first court appearance at the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal. Mr. Vasiljevic, a 45-year-old former paramilitary fighter, was arrested by NATO forces on Tuesday. He pleaded not guilty.   Marlise Simons
news.title: World Briefing

news.abstract: Criminal inquiry into campaign practices of Prime Min Ehud Barak threatens to undermine Israelis' trust in him and his ability to make peace with Arabs without compromising security; Barak himself was not implicated by comptroller's report, which found that his associates systematically channeled illegal contributions through nonprofit organizations, but comptroller did hold him responsible for their actions, and a new poll shows that a majority believe Barak was well aware of what they were doing (M)
news.title: Tainted Trust and Mideast Peace

news.abstract: Pres Clinton appeals to chief executives and national leaders attending World Economic Forum, Davos, Switzerland, to make global trade work for poor; warns failure to listen to concerns of those who have not benefited from globalization would spur protectionism; demonstrators, kept away from forum site, break windows in nearby McDonald's restaurant; forum organizers increase security; photo (M)
news.title: At Trade Forum, Clinton Pleads for the Poor

news.abstract: American-based Chinese scholar Song Yongyi arrives back in United States after being jailed in China for nearly six months; holds he was mentally tortured by security agents who demanded he confess to espionage and implicate others, news conference and interview; credits release to pressure from Congress and from western scholars; photo (M)
news.title: Scholar Back in U.S. After China Detention

news.abstract: Russian mothers seek advice on strategies to help sons evade draft legally; demand for help has grown with increaded fighting in Chechnya; photo (M)
